prompt: A policy allows `s3:ListBucket` on `arn:aws:s3:::shop-assets/*` and `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::shop-assets`. What can its holder do?
hint: Which action acts on the bucket, and which on its objects?

choices.text: Both, since the bucket's ARN covers the objects inside it
choices.why: The bucket and its objects are separate resources with separate ARNs; neither covers the other.

choices.text: List the bucket, but not read its objects
choices.why: Listing is an action on the bucket, and this policy gives it only on objects, so listing fails too.

choices.text: Neither: each action names the wrong kind of resource
choices.why: Right. The two resources are swapped, so the policy grants nothing it meant to. bia's policy pairs `ListBucket` with the bucket and the object actions with `shop-assets/*`.

choices.text: Nothing, because AWS refuses the document as malformed
choices.why: The document is well formed: every element is valid. It is wrong in meaning, which no grammar check sees.

prompt: What is `2012-10-17` in a policy's `Version` line?
hint: It is the same in every policy you write.

choices.text: The date the policy was first written
choices.why: It does not change with your documents. A policy written today carries the same date.

choices.text: The date AWS fixed the grammar
choices.why: Right. It is the date AWS fixed the language; the older `2008-10-17` lacks policy variables, and a document without the line is read as the older one.

choices.text: The version number AWS shows as `v1`, `v2` and so on
choices.why: Those are versions of a managed policy, kept by IAM. The `Version` element is inside every one of them, unchanged.

choices.text: The release of the IAM API the command line calls
choices.why: The API has a version of its own in every request. The policy's `Version` is about the language of the document.

prompt: A statement allows `s3:Get*` on every resource. Next year AWS adds a new S3 operation whose name begins with `Get`. Does the statement allow it?
hint: When is the wildcard compared with the action's name?

choices.text: No: a wildcard is expanded into a fixed list when the policy is saved
choices.why: Nothing is expanded at save time. The pattern is matched against the action of each request as it arrives.

choices.text: Yes, from the day it exists, with no edit to the policy
choices.why: Right. The pattern matches names, including names that did not exist when it was written, which is the reason to think before writing one.

choices.text: Only after somebody publishes a new version of the policy
choices.why: A new version changes the document; it is not needed for an old pattern to match a new name.

choices.text: Only if the policy is AWS-managed, since AWS updates those itself
choices.why: AWS does edit its own policies, but a wildcard in yours matches the new name without anybody editing anything.

prompt: Two policies are identical except that one lists its `Deny` statement before its `Allow` statement and the other after it. How do they differ in effect?
hint: Is a policy read like a firewall?

choices.text: The first match wins, so the first policy denies and the second allows
choices.why: That is a firewall's rule. IAM considers every statement together, whatever their order.

choices.text: The last statement wins, as in a configuration file
choices.why: Nothing is overridden by position. Lesson 8 gives the rule that does settle them.

choices.text: In nothing: IAM has no order among statements
choices.why: Right. The statements are a set, and lesson 8 settles them by effect, never by position.

choices.text: Statements are applied in the alphabetical order of their `Sid`
choices.why: A `Sid` is only a label, and optional. It never decides anything.

prompt: The element that names who a trust policy trusts, and that an identity policy leaves out, is called ___.
hint: It appeared in lesson 6's trust policy, with `AWS` or `Federated` inside it.

prompt: moto is started with `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT=3`. A student first runs `aws sts get-caller-identity` to see that it answers, then the three bootstrap commands. How many of the three bootstrap commands get through unchecked?
hint: Every request counts, whatever it asks.

prompt: In the bootstrap, `aws iam list-users` came fourth and was refused with `InvalidClientTokenId`. Why?
hint: What was the terminal still signing with at that moment?

choices.text: admin had no permission to list users yet
choices.why: admin already held `AdministratorAccess`. But the request was not signed as admin at all.

choices.text: It was signed with `test`, a key moto's IAM never issued
choices.why: Right. The three free requests were spent, so the fourth was checked, and `test` belongs to nobody. The `export` line fixes it.

choices.text: The new access key takes a minute to become active
choices.why: moto's keys are active at once, and the new key had not been used yet in any case.

choices.text: moto refuses `list-users` once its checking is on
choices.why: Three commands later the same call, signed with admin's key, listed the users.

prompt: Which of these requests does NOT spend one of the free requests of `INITIAL_NO_AUTH_ACTION_COUNT`?
hint: One address belongs to moto itself, not to the AWS it imitates.

choices.text: A request that fails with an error
choices.why: A failure still counts, which is how a typo in the bootstrap ruins it.

choices.text: `aws sts get-caller-identity`
choices.why: It reaches moto's AWS API like any other call, so it is counted like any other.

choices.text: A request to moto's own `/moto-api/` address
choices.why: Right. That is moto's control address, outside the AWS it imitates, and the command line never sends anything there.

choices.text: A request sent from the first terminal instead of the second
choices.why: moto counts requests, not terminals; where it was typed makes no difference.

prompt: After the bootstrap, a student opens a third terminal, reads `env.sh` and runs `aws iam list-users`. It is refused. What is the right fix?
hint: What does `env.sh` set the keys to, and where does `key` live?

choices.text: Restart moto, since a new terminal resets the count
choices.why: The count is moto's and has nothing to do with terminals. Restarting would throw away admin and everything else.

choices.text: Write admin's key into `env.sh`, so every terminal starts with it
choices.why: A key in a file is the habit this course refuses, even for moto's worthless keys: the habit is what reaches a real one.

choices.text: Use the shell where admin's key is exported
choices.why: Right. The new terminal signs with `test`, which moto now refuses, and the variable `key` exists only in the old shell.

choices.text: Attach `AdministratorAccess` to the user `test`
choices.why: There is no user `test`: it is a key moto's IAM never issued, and no policy makes it one.

prompt: What does `with_key "$bia" aws s3 ls` change in the terminal?
hint: Look at where the two variables are set inside the function.

choices.text: Only that one command is signed with bia's key
choices.why: Right. The variables are set in front of the command, so they last for that command alone, and the next one is admin's again.

choices.text: It switches the terminal to bia until the shell exits
choices.why: That is what `export` does, as in the bootstrap. The function never exports anything.

choices.text: It creates a new access key for bia each time it runs
choices.why: It reads the key already kept in `$bia`; creating one would be `create-access-key`, run once.

choices.text: It asks moto to act as bia without signing the request
choices.why: Every request is signed; the function only chooses which key signs this one.

prompt: An external auditor is given `ReadOnlyAccess` in the shop's account. What can the auditor now see?
hint: Read the S3 lines of its default version.

choices.text: The settings of each service, but not the data inside them
choices.why: `s3:Get*` includes `GetObject`, which is the data itself.

choices.text: Every object in every bucket, the backups included
choices.why: Right. Read-only is a promise about writing. For an auditor, a customer-managed policy naming what the audit needs is the narrower answer.

choices.text: Only what the shop adds to the policy later
choices.why: The shop cannot edit an AWS-managed policy. AWS does, and has 188 times.

choices.text: The list of buckets, but no object in any of them
choices.why: `s3:List*` gives the lists, and `s3:Get*` gives the objects as well.

prompt: Which of these ARNs is an AWS-managed policy?
hint: Look where the account number would be.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:policy/shop-assets-rw`
choices.why: That one carries the shop's account: it is customer-managed.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::123456789012:user/admin`
choices.why: That is a user, not a policy.

choices.text: `arn:aws:s3:::shop-assets`
choices.why: That is a bucket, with neither account nor region in its ARN.

choices.text: `arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess`
choices.why: Right: `aws` in the account's place, which is how every account can name the same policy.

prompt: `shop-assets-rw` already has five versions. Put in order the steps to publish an edit safely and undo it if it is wrong.
hint: There is no room for a sixth.
items: delete the oldest version that is not the default
try the change as the user who holds the policy
if it is wrong, `set-default-policy-version` back to the previous one
trap: Creating first is the usual slip: at five versions it is refused with `LimitExceeded`, before anything changes.

prompt: bia's request to delete an object came back `Access Denied`. A colleague says her key must be wrong. What does the error tell you?
hint: Compare it with the error the `test` key got.

choices.text: That the key is wrong, as S3 words every failure the same way
choices.why: A key moto never issued got `InvalidClientTokenId` in the bootstrap. S3 has its own word for a bad key too.

choices.text: That the key passed, and nothing allowed the deletion
choices.why: Right. Access Denied comes after the signature is checked; her policy never named `s3:DeleteObject`.

choices.text: That the object does not exist
choices.why: `logo.txt` was there; bia had just read it. A missing object is a different answer.

choices.text: That moto does not implement deleting objects
choices.why: moto deletes objects for whoever is allowed to; the refusal came from the policy check.

prompt: Why does the lesson list objects with `s3api list-objects-v2` rather than `aws s3 ls s3://shop-assets`?
hint: admin got the same answer as bia would.

choices.text: `aws s3 ls` needs `s3:ListAllMyBuckets`, which bia lacks
choices.why: That permission is for listing the buckets, `aws s3 ls` with no address. And admin, who has everything, was refused too.

choices.text: moto refuses its signature, whoever signs; AWS accepts both
choices.why: Right. The `/` delimiter it sends trips moto's signature check, so the answer is `SignatureDoesNotMatch` even for admin.

choices.text: `aws s3 ls` is deprecated in AWS CLI version 2
choices.why: It is current and works against AWS; the problem was moto's.

choices.text: bia's policy allows `s3api` calls but not `s3` calls
choices.why: A policy names API actions, and both commands call the same `ListObjectsV2` action.

prompt: A customer-managed policy has versions `v1` to `v5`, with `v1` the default. How many versions must be deleted before two new versions can be created?
hint: The limit counts every version, the default included.

prompt: `aws iam delete-user --user-name edu` answers `DeleteConflict ... must delete policies first`. What does that mean?
hint: Which kind of policy lives inside the user?

choices.text: The policy is attached to other users, who would lose it
choices.why: An inline policy belongs to edu alone; nobody else can hold it.

choices.text: edu still holds an inline policy, and it has to be deleted first
choices.why: Right. The API names each inline policy before the user goes, and once both are deleted there is no copy to reuse.

choices.text: A deleted user is kept for a week, and the policy with him
choices.why: There is no waiting period; `get-user` answered `NoSuchEntity` straight after.

choices.text: The inline policy will survive the user and stay attachable
choices.why: That is what a managed policy does. An inline one has no ARN to survive by.

prompt: Thirty roles need the same permission, which must be changed in one place and rolled back quickly if a change is wrong. Which kind of policy fits?
hint: Count the places an edit would have to be made.

choices.text: An inline policy in each role, so that none of them shares it
choices.why: Thirty copies are thirty edits, with no versions to roll back to.

choices.text: An inline policy in a group, with the roles in that group
choices.why: A group holds users, never roles, so the roles cannot join it.

choices.text: A single customer-managed document, attached to every one of them
choices.why: Right. One document, one edit, and a rollback that is a change of default version.

choices.text: AWS's `PowerUserAccess`, which AWS keeps current for everyone
choices.why: It is not this permission, and its changes are AWS's, on AWS's schedule, with no rollback of yours.

prompt: Match each need to the kind of policy the lesson recommends.
hint: The last row of the table.

pairs.left: a permission that must never reach a second identity
a job function AWS describes and keeps current
the shop's own permission, shared and versioned

prompt: Which of these are true of an inline policy on a user? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare it with `shop-assets-rw`.

choices.text: It has a name but no ARN
choices.why: Right, which is why nothing else can name it to attach it.

choices.text: It can be attached to a second user
choices.why: It is written into one identity; another gets its own copy or nothing.

choices.text: An edit overwrites it, with no earlier version kept
choices.why: Right. Versions belong to managed policies only.

choices.text: It may hold 6,144 characters
choices.why: That is the limit of a managed policy; a user's inline policies stop at 2,048.

choices.text: It is gone once the user is deleted
choices.why: Right. The API makes you delete it first, and then there is nothing left.

prompt: moto accepted an identity policy with a `Principal` element and obeyed it. Before the same policy is used in a real account, what should be done?
hint: moto's acceptance is not AWS's.

choices.text: Nothing, because moto obeyed it and moto answers as AWS does
choices.why: moto answers in AWS's format and checks less. AWS refuses this document before storing it.

choices.text: Make it customer-managed, since managed policies accept a `Principal`
choices.why: Every identity policy is refused with a `Principal`, managed or inline: the principal is whoever it is attached to.

choices.text: Remove `Principal` and validate against AWS's grammar
choices.why: Right. Lesson 8 names IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation as that check; moto answers it with an error, so it runs against AWS.

choices.text: Change its `Version` to `2008-10-17`, which allows a `Principal`
choices.why: The old language lacks policy variables; it does not make an identity policy accept a principal.

prompt: `aws iam list-user-policies --user-name caio` prints an empty list, yet caio reads every bucket. Where should you look next?
hint: That command lists one kind of policy only.

choices.text: His attached managed policies, and those of his groups
choices.why: Right. `list-user-policies` shows inline ones; `list-attached-user-policies` and `list-groups-for-user` show the rest.

choices.text: Nowhere: an empty list means he holds no policy
choices.why: It means he holds no inline policy. Half of what a user can do is in the other list.

choices.text: At the buckets' own settings, since S3 is open by default
choices.why: A new bucket is private. Something gave caio access, and it is in IAM first.

choices.text: At moto's count, which may still be letting him through
choices.why: The three free requests were spent in the bootstrap; every request since is judged.

prompt: A managed policy keeps at most ___ versions.
hint: `LimitExceeded` said the number.
